name: mbelib
why: A P25 digital voice vocoder that turns radio bitstreams into speech, a real transform into audio from the radio world.

brief.what_it_is: mbelib is a C library for the MBE family of speech codecs, the vocoders used in digital radio. The README says it supports the 7200x4400 bit/s codec used in P25 Phase 1, the 7100x4400 bit/s codec used in ProVoice, and the half-rate 3600x2250 bit/s vocoder used in various radio systems. The README does not spell out the input and output formats in detail, so the decode direction (bitstream in, speech out) comes from the scout notes rather than the README. It is built with CMake and installs as a library.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the code as educational: it is 'a written description of how certain voice encoding/decoding algorythims could be implemented.' It exists so people can work with the P25 and ProVoice voice codecs in software.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internal mechanism. It only names the supported codec bit rates and frame sizes and gives build steps.

commands_seen.context: Refreshes package lists before installing build tools on Ubuntu (the README's comment says 'Update packages').

commands_seen.cmd: sudo apt-get install git make cmake
commands_seen.context: Installs git, make and cmake, the tools needed to fetch and build the library on Ubuntu.
Clones the repo; the README leaves the URL as a placeholder, with an example of git@github.com:USERNAME/mbelib.git.
Moves into the cloned source folder.
Creates a build directory for an out-of-source CMake build.
Generates a Makefile for the current system from the parent directory's CMake files.
Compiles the library (per the README's comment).
Installs the compiled library into the system.

brief.install_notes: The README gives only an Ubuntu example: install git, make and cmake with apt, clone the repo, then run mkdir build, cd build, cmake .., make and sudo make install. Nothing is said about hardware, accounts or runtimes. The README is not a Homebrew guide, so brew install is not covered here. The Travis CI badge suggests the project was built in CI at some point.
brief.standout: Unusually, the README opens with a patent notice that says the source is for educational purposes and that compiled executables may be covered by patents. Few libraries lead with a legal warning like this, and it shapes how the project should be read and used.
brief.status: Unknown. The README names version 1.3.0 but gives no release date. I did not check the commit history or releases page, so I cannot confirm recent activity. The Travis CI badge points to travis-ci.org, a service that has since been retired, which hints the project's CI setup is old.
brief.caveats: Patent notice in the README: the source is provided for educational purposes only, and executables compiled or derived from it may be covered by one or more patents. Users are told to check patent restrictions and licensing before compiling or using it. The README gives no license name. The install example is Ubuntu-only and has a placeholder clone URL. The README does not explain what input the library expects, so the decode direction is unconfirmed from the README itself.
